description: My name is Christopher Schleyer, and I am a senior Computer Science major with a minor in Mathematics at Stockton University. My interest in computer hardware started in high school when I built my first desktop computer for schoolwork and gaming, around the same time I earned my Eagle Scout rank. I currently enjoy developing useful web applications and have experience with Python, Java, SQL, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Bash, and Git.
summary:
MarsPath is my entry for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. It’s a prototype mission-planning interface for human exploration of Mars, built with Java, Spring Boot, Maven, JSON, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

A Spring Boot REST API serves Mars location data as JSON to a JavaScript front end. When the app starts, it shows three notable sites: Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Olympus Mons. For each, users can search, read scientific details, explore NASA orbital imagery with zoom controls, and plan a route between sites.

The maps use real data from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (CTX camera mosaics), downloaded from NASA’s Mars Trek. Because the raw GeoTIFFs are several gigabytes, a separate Python script (rasterio, Pillow, NumPy; not part of the app) downsamples them and applies a contrast stretch to produce lightweight PNGs for display.

As a prototype, MarsPath currently shows one optical data layer. Next steps: topographic and thermal layers, terrain-aware walking routes within a site such as Jezero’s delta, and a radiation and weather safety panel.
details:
What it does: MarsPath is a prototype planning display a crew could use inside a habitat to review exploration sites on Mars. A Spring Boot REST API serves location data as JSON to a JavaScript front end. Users can search three sites (Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Olympus Mons), read each site’s region, status, description, and scientific interest, explore NASA orbital imagery with zoom controls, and choose a start and destination to estimate the distance between sites.

Data: The maps are real MRO CTX mosaics from NASA/JPL’s Mars Trek. The raw GeoTIFFs are very large (up to 10.7 GB), so I wrote a separate Python script (rasterio, Pillow, NumPy; not part of the app) that downsamples them and applies a contrast stretch to produce lightweight PNGs for display.

Benefits and intended impact: MarsPath brings site information, imagery, and route planning into one interface instead of spreading them across separate tools. It’s meant as a foundation for the hyperlocal, layered maps that human Mars missions will need, and it gives the public an approachable way to explore real Mars data.

Tools: Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5, Maven, JSON (Jackson), HTML, CSS, JavaScript, the Eclipse IDE, and Python. I also used AI assistants (ChatGPT and Claude) for parts of the front-end code and for troubleshooting.

Creativity: I framed Mars data as a crew-facing planning tool, not just an image viewer. The REST design means new sites can be added by editing the JSON data file instead of the code. The conversion script makes multi-gigabyte NASA data usable in a browser.

Factors considered: Storage and performance (raw data kept outside the project, web-sized display copies), Mars coordinate conventions (east longitude, 0–360°), and distance on a sphere instead of a flat grid. The display images are not for measurement. Since astronaut safety is NASA’s first priority, my next steps are topographic and thermal layers, hazard-aware walking routes in Jezero using HiRISE imagery, and a radiation and weather safety panel.
